quotes.text: The Hold Steady emerged with riff-heavy, piano-accented anthems that drew on Finn's youthful, Middle American misadventures.
Right when everyone else was enraptured with leather jackets and Duran Duran, The Hold Steady waved the flag for cheap beer and Bob Seger.
Over time, a band that once commented on classic-rock clichés with wit and insight now seemed to embody them.

Open Door Policy integrates the more layered production of Finn's solo records (steered by excellent indie producer of the moment Josh Kaufman) into The Hold Steady's bedrock, rough-and-tumble sound. The result suits this battle-scarred though ultimately lovable band — it's their most mature record and one of their darkest, but it also evinces the genuine joy that's enabled them to endure.

Then a few months later, we had six more. It was two different weekends. There was a real party atmosphere in the studio. There was a looseness to it that I really love.
Everything else culturally was bands with tight pants and making indie rockers dance again, that kind of thing. We were like, "What if we bummed everyone out?"
To come out with a down-in-the-middle rock record, I think people looked at it in a certain way that ended up being really helpful.

Four albums on (really six for vocalist Craig Finn and guitarist Tad Kubler, holdovers from Lifter Puller), the band have established themselves enough to hit the road wherever they damn well please. Their status as veterans is absolutely pervasive here, whether it's the gall to take an indulgent solo or a comment about the independent music scene writ large.
Rather than slacken up, Craig Finn reached deep and wrote 11 of the most harrowing, clever, and profound songs backed by a band ever-tightening their chops.

Lyrically, Finn is at the top of his craft. While nothing about his songwriting is drastically different, he ditches the Charlemagne, Holly, and Gideon characters; much like John Darnielle has left his Alpha couple and "Going to" crutches.

Musically, this is the most sophisticated THS album yet. The fairly hackneyed chord progression on "Lord, I'm Discouraged" makes dramatic sense when it's rescued by a wicked Kubler solo; joining the wah-drenched effort on "Joke About Jamaica" as far and away the two best guitar solos in The Hold Steady catalogue.

Franz Nicolay pounds on piano, organ, harpsichord, and even Lifter Puller synths, in order of increasing bizarre charm. The production is notable in that it simply lets the band's sound breathe, rather than hanging on any kind of contrived atmosphere.
The aforementioned new keyboard sounds, theremin and heavier use of horns nearing on Sufjan levels on "Magazines" are the big changes.

Stay Positive staves off the pitfalls inherent to creative (and increasingly commercial) success facing The Hold Steady after Boys and Girls in America. It is a more mature record from a more mature band, and still a net improvement from the raw, sloppy first two albums.
